title: Why Did the Bronze Serpent Bring Healing?
paragraphs:
Why Did the Bronze Serpent Bring Healing?
The Scandalous Symbol That Pointed to the Cross Before the Cross Ever Existed
There are moments in Scripture that feel almost impossible to understand.
Moments that seem to collide headfirst with everything we think we know about God.
The bronze serpent is one of them.
If you read the story too quickly, you might miss how shocking it really is.
God had forbidden idolatry.
God repeatedly warned Israel not to worship images.
God condemned the serpent in Eden as the instrument Satan used to deceive humanity.
Yet somehow, in one of the strangest moments in biblical history, God commanded Moses to make a serpent out of bronze and lift it high above the people.
And whoever looked at it lived.
At first glance, it almost feels backwards.
Why would a symbol of judgment become a symbol of healing?
Why would God use a serpent—the very image associated with humanity's fall—to save dying people?
And why would Jesus Himself later compare this event to His own crucifixion?
The answer reaches deeper than most people realize.
It is a story about rebellion.
A story about judgment.
A story about grace.
And ultimately, a story about Jesus Christ.
The account appears in Numbers 21:4-9.
Israel had been miraculously delivered from Egypt.
God had split the Red Sea.
Fed them with manna.
Guided them by a pillar of cloud and fire.
Protected them repeatedly.
Yet despite witnessing miracle after miracle, the people became impatient.
Their hearts grew bitter.
Their gratitude vanished.
Their worship became complaint.
Numbers 21:5 records their words:
"And the people spoke against God and against Moses, 'Why have you brought us up out of Egypt to die in the wilderness? For there is no bread and no water, and we loathe this worthless food.'"
The Hebrew phrase translated "spoke against" carries the idea of hostile rebellion.
This was not frustration.
This was open defiance.
The people were rejecting God's provision while simultaneously surviving because of it.
How often do we do the same?
We complain about the very blessings keeping us alive.
We resent the provisions we once prayed for.
We demand more while forgetting what God has already done.
Israel's story suddenly becomes our story.
The wilderness simply exposes what already exists inside the human heart.
Then judgment came.
Numbers 21:6 says:
"Then the LORD sent fiery serpents among the people, and they bit the people, so that many people of Israel died."
The Hebrew term is שְׂרָפִים (seraphim).
Literally, "burning ones."
Most likely referring to the intense burning sensation caused by their venom.
The same root appears elsewhere for heavenly beings called seraphim, emphasizing something blazing or burning.
The snakes became visible reminders of invisible sin.
What had been hidden inside their hearts suddenly became impossible to ignore.
Every bite revealed a deeper reality.
Rebellion kills.
Sin destroys.
Disobedience always carries consequences.
The people quickly recognized their guilt.
Numbers 21:7 records:
"We have sinned."
In Hebrew:
חָטָאנוּ (chatanu)
"We have sinned."
A confession.
Not an excuse.
Not blame shifting.
Not self-justification.
Simply an acknowledgment of guilt.
Something our culture often struggles to do.
The people begged Moses to intercede.
And then God gave a solution no one could have predicted.
Numbers 21:8:
"Make a fiery serpent and set it on a pole, and everyone who is bitten, when he sees it, shall live."
The Hebrew word for pole is:
נֵס (nes)
A banner.
A standard.
Something lifted high for everyone to see.
Moses obeyed.
He crafted a bronze serpent.
In Hebrew:
נְחַשׁ נְחֹשֶׁת (nachash nechoshet)
A fascinating wordplay.
"Serpent of bronze."
The words sound remarkably similar.
Ancient Hebrew listeners would have immediately noticed the connection.
Then came the astonishing promise:
Anyone who looked would live.
Not anyone who deserved it.
Not anyone who earned it.
Not anyone who paid for it.
Anyone who looked.
Imagine the scene.
Thousands suffering.
Families grieving.
Panic spreading throughout the camp.
Venom moving through veins.
People collapsing.
Death everywhere.
And standing in the middle of the crisis was God's unexpected answer.
Look.
Live.
Refuse.
Die.
The healing itself was not in the bronze.
The power was not in the metal.
The serpent was not magical.
The healing came through trusting God's promise.
Looking became an act of faith.
A visible expression of invisible trust.
And this is where the story becomes breathtaking.
More than a thousand years later, Jesus referenced this exact event.
Speaking to Nicodemus, He said:
"And as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up." (John 3:14)
The Greek reads:
Καὶ καθὼς Μωϋσῆς ὕψωσεν τὸν ὄφιν ἐν τῇ ἐρήμῳ, οὕτως ὑψωθῆναι δεῖ τὸν Υἱὸν τοῦ ἀνθρώπου.
Jesus deliberately connected Himself to the bronze serpent.
Not because He was sinful.
He was sinless.
Not because He was cursed in His nature.
He was holy.
But because He would become the bearer of judgment on behalf of sinners.
Paul explains this mystery:
"For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin." (2 Corinthians 5:21)
And again:
"Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us." (Galatians 3:13)
The bronze serpent represented the very thing killing the people.
Likewise, Christ bore the very judgment that was killing humanity.
This is the scandal of the Gospel.
God defeated sin by placing its judgment upon His Son.
The serpent lifted high symbolized judgment exposed.
The cross lifted high revealed judgment satisfied.
At Calvary, Jesus became what the bronze serpent foreshadowed.
Not sinful.
But carrying sin.
Not cursed by His own actions.
But bearing our curse.
Not guilty.
But standing in the place of the guilty.
The bronze serpent was never the final answer.
It was a shadow.
Jesus is the substance.
The serpent healed physical death.
Christ heals spiritual death.
The serpent saved bodies.
Christ saves souls.
The serpent offered temporary relief.
Jesus offers eternal life.
That is why John 3:15 immediately follows:
"That whoever believes in him may have eternal life."
Notice the similarity.
In Numbers, they looked and lived.
In John, they believe and live.
Faith has always been the means.
Salvation has always been God's work.
Grace has always been the answer.
Yet the story becomes even more fascinating.
Centuries later, Israel turned the bronze serpent into an idol.
They began worshipping it.
2 Kings 18:4 records that King Hezekiah destroyed it.
He called it:
נְחֻשְׁתָּן (Nehushtan)
Essentially saying:
"It's just a piece of bronze."
The object that once pointed people to God had become a replacement for God.
The symbol became more important than the Savior.
Humanity still struggles with the same temptation.
We cling to religious symbols.
Church traditions.
Denominational identities.
Personal achievements.
Good works.
Spiritual experiences.
And sometimes we forget the One they were supposed to point toward.
The bronze serpent was never the hero.
Jesus is.
The cross itself is not the hero.
Jesus is.
The church is not the hero.
Jesus is.
The preacher is not the hero.
Jesus is.
The ministry is not the hero.
Jesus is.
Every symbol, every prophecy, every sacrifice, every miracle, every page of Scripture ultimately points to one Person.
Jesus Christ.
And perhaps that is why this ancient story still grips us today.
Because deep down, we know what it feels like to carry venom.
Maybe not from a snake.
But from shame.
Regret.
Addiction.
Pride.
Bitterness.
Secrets.
Failures.
Scars.
Things we wish nobody knew.
Things we hope never come into the light.
We know what it feels like to realize we cannot heal ourselves.
To discover that self-improvement is not enough.
To reach the end of our strength.
That is exactly where God's grace meets us.
The Israelites could not remove the poison.
They could only look.
We cannot save ourselves.
We can only look to Christ.
The Gospel is not a story about people climbing up to God.
It is the story of God coming down to rescue people who could never climb high enough.
That is why the bronze serpent remains one of the most powerful pictures of redemption in all Scripture.
It whispers the Gospel long before Bethlehem.
It foreshadows Calvary long before the nails.
It points to resurrection long before the empty tomb.
It reminds us that God specializes in transforming symbols of shame into testimonies of grace.
And perhaps that describes your story too.
Maybe your past feels like a scandal.
Maybe your mistakes seem too great.
Maybe your failures still haunt you.
Maybe your wounds are deeper than anyone realizes.
The enemy wants you to believe your story is finished.
Jesus says otherwise.
Because the entire Bible tells one consistent story:
God takes what sin destroys and transforms it through grace.
A serpent became a symbol of healing.
A cross became a symbol of salvation.
A grave became a symbol of victory.
And broken sinners become redeemed sons and daughters of God.
That is the heartbeat of the Gospel Warrior mission.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
You may never know whose life is changed because you chose to share biblical truth.
Have you ever experienced a season where Jesus turned something painful, shameful, or broken into a testimony of grace?

Your support helps expand Gospel-centered content that reaches people with biblical truth, discipleship, encouragement, and hope. Supporting the ministry is one practical way believers participate in spreading the Gospel and helping others encounter Jesus.
One look at the serpent healed a dying body—one look at Christ can change an eternal destiny.
